source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Moore_2007_PsychoticAffectiveOutcomesSR.pdf (Lancet 2007;370:319-28, version of record), all 10 pages, pp. 319-328: full text extracted with pdftotext -layout; Figures 1-2 and Table 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi (pp. 320-322); Figures 3-6 and Table 2 read from the text layer. Not read: webtables 1-2 (online supplement) and the authors' departmental website.

claims.note: Moore-sourced parts checked: the attenuation 'about 45% (10% to 80%)' of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts is printed on p. 322 (text) and per cohort in Table 1; the mean of the seven Table 1 values is 310/7 = 44.3%, same as 'about 45%'. 'Excess odds' is right: Table 1's footnote defines the change as (crude OR - adjusted OR)/(crude OR - 1). Caveat for the editor: Table 1 does not say which exposure contrast each percentage refers to, and for NPMS the 80% cannot refer to the ever-use estimate of Figure 1 (adjusted OR 0.72 would mean more than 100% attenuation); it fits the dependence estimate (1.47, Figure 2) with a crude OR near 3.4, so the seven percentages may mix ever-use and frequency contrasts. 'Consistent and stronger with frequent use' matches p. 321. Omission rather than overstatement: Moore et al. read their own results as consistent with cannabis raising risk independently of confounding and as enough to warn young people (p. 319, p. 327); the claim lists only narrative reviews' readings and attributes the public-health-message reading to Gage 2016 and Murray 2016.

anchors.locator: Table 1, column 'Approximate change from crude to adjusted OR (%)', and its footnote
anchors.extracted: Per-cohort reduction from crude to adjusted OR: CHDS 65%, Dunedin 10%, ECA 30%, EDSP 15%, NEMESIS 50%, NPMS 80%, Swedish conscripts 60%; change defined as (crude OR - adjusted OR)/(crude OR - 1), i.e. share of the excess odds removed; CHDS and Dunedin figures from extra data supplied by investigators. Mean of the seven 44.3% (second reader's calculation); exposure contrast behind each figure not stated.

anchors.locator: Results, right column, paragraph beginning 'The studies listed in table 1 adjusted for about 60 different confounding factors'
anchors.extracted: About 60 confounders across the seven cohorts (other substance use, personality traits, sociodemographic markers, intellectual ability, other mental health problems); in every study the fully adjusted estimate was smaller than the crude one, by about 45% on average (range 10% to 80%); fixed-effects regression in CHDS for unmeasured time-invariant confounders changed little; adjusting for other substance use attenuated ECA and NEMESIS substantially; in the Swedish conscripts IQ, urban upbringing and other mental disorders were the strongest confounders.

anchors.locator: Results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (left column) and Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Crude estimates showed raised risk in all seven studies; after adjustment the association was reduced but persisted in six. Pooled adjusted OR for any psychotic outcome after ever use 1.41 (1.20-1.65; I2 19.2%); all six studies that looked at frequency (linear trend or higher vs lower category) were consistent with a dose-response; most frequent use vs none 2.09 (1.54-2.84; I2 44.1%).

anchors.locator: Summary (Interpretation); Discussion, 2nd column of p. 325 (confounding paragraph); concluding paragraph of the Discussion on p. 327
anchors.extracted: Authors' reading: evidence consistent with cannabis raising risk of psychotic outcomes independently of confounding and transient intoxication, and sufficient to warn young people; at the same time residual confounding can never be eliminated, confounding or bias cannot be ruled out, and the uncertainty is unlikely to be resolved by further longitudinal studies. Random misclassification of exposure and attrition would bias towards the null (pp. 325-326).

claims.note: Every Moore figure in the statement and magnitude matches the PDF (checked on rendered pp. 320-322): 1.41 (1.20-1.65), I2 19.2%; 2.09 (1.54-2.84), I2 44.1%, and 1.92 (1.50-2.47) without NEMESIS; 2.58 (1.08-6.13), I2 66.9%, and 1.82 (1.01-3.30) without NEMESIS; about 60 confounders; about 45% (10%-80%) attenuation; three of the six most-frequent-use estimates (EDSP, NEMESIS, NPMS) not adjusted for other drug use; the frequency categories (>50 times, weekly, daily, dependence) are as in Figure 2. Small points: (1) the ever-use exposure was past-year use in NPMS (Figure 1 legend), so 'ever use against never use' holds for six of seven; (2) the statement that no source gives absolute risks by level of use, and that the reviews give absolute figures only as calculations assuming causality, overlooks Moore's own figure: lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, even with regular use, 'likely to be low (less than 3%)' (p. 327), stated without derivation, and a population attributable fraction of about 14% (7-19) that is explicitly conditional on causality (p. 326). Neither changes the claim's substance, but the sentence on absolute figures should mention Moore or be softened. (3) Moore's Discussion says all studies reporting an association adjusted for other drug use (p. 325), which sits uneasily with Figure 2's footnote; the claim follows the footnote, which is the more specific statement.

anchors.locator: Figure 1 and its legend (p. 320); Results, 2nd paragraph of left column (p. 321)
anchors.extracted: Any psychotic outcome after ever use, adjusted ORs: CHDS 1.28 (1.04-1.57), Dunedin schizophreniform 2.91 (1.20-7.04), ECA 1.30 (0.98-1.73), EDSP 1.67 (1.13-2.46), NEMESIS 2.11 (0.78-5.71), NPMS 0.72 (0.30-1.74), Swedish schizophrenia 1.50 (1.11-2.02); random-effects pooled 1.41 (1.20-1.65), heterogeneity p = 0.28, I2 19.2%; pooled on the assumption of a continuum from self-reported symptoms to clinical schizophrenia; exposure ever use except NPMS (use in the past year). Outcome instruments (Table 1, p. 322): SCL-90 self-report (CHDS), PSQ questionnaire (NPMS), DIS/CIDI/M-CIDI interviews (Dunedin, ECA, NEMESIS, EDSP), ICD hospital diagnosis (Swedish).

anchors.locator: Figure 2 and footnote; Results, 3rd paragraph of left column
anchors.extracted: Most frequent use vs none, adjusted ORs: CHDS daily 1.56 (1.20-2.03), ECA daily 2.00 (1.27-3.16), EDSP daily 2.23 (1.30-3.83), NEMESIS weekly 6.81 (1.79-25.91), NPMS dependence 1.47 (0.55-3.93), Swedish >50 times 3.10 (1.72-5.58); pooled 2.09 (1.54-2.84), heterogeneity p = 0.11, I2 44.1%; EDSP, NEMESIS and NPMS estimates not adjusted for other drug use; all six studies examining frequency reported findings consistent with a dose-response.

anchors.locator: Results, last paragraph of left column and 1st paragraph of right column
anchors.extracted: Psychotic disorder (Swedish schizophrenia, Dunedin schizophreniform disorder, NEMESIS needs-based diagnosis), ever use: pooled adjusted OR 2.58 (1.08-6.13), heterogeneity p = 0.049, I2 66.9%. Omitting NEMESIS (largest contributor to heterogeneity): most frequent use 1.92 (1.50-2.47; p = 0.26; I2 25.0%), psychotic disorder 1.82 (1.01-3.30; p = 0.16; I2 48.3%).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (last column) and Results, right column, paragraph beginning 'The studies listed in table 1'
anchors.extracted: About 60 confounders adjusted across studies (other substance use, personality traits, sociodemographic markers, intellectual ability, other mental health problems); adjusted estimates attenuated from crude by about 45% on average, range 10%-80% (per cohort 65, 10, 30, 15, 50, 80, 60%).

anchors.locator: Results, right column, paragraph on age of first use (p. 321); Discussion, left column, 3rd paragraph (p. 325)
anchors.extracted: Two cohorts examined age at first use: Dunedin found a stronger association with symptoms for first use before 16, with much weaker evidence and very wide intervals for schizophreniform disorder; the Swedish conscripts showed no difference before vs after 16 with cumulative use taken into account. The review concludes that no robust evidence supports greater harm from earlier use and that Dunedin's pattern could reflect greater cumulative exposure.

anchors.locator: Discussion, left column of p. 326 (attributable fraction); concluding paragraph of the Discussion on p. 327
anchors.extracted: Assuming causality, an OR of 1.4 and about 40% ever use among UK young adults, about 14% (95% CI 7-19) of psychotic outcomes in young adults would not occur without cannabis. Separately, the authors state without derivation that individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, even with regular use, is likely to be low (less than 3%).

Authors state that all studies reporting an association for psychosis adjusted for other drug use, two (NEMESIS, Dunedin) did not adjust for alcohol, and three (EDSP, NEMESIS, Dunedin) did not adjust for other mental disorders at baseline; this differs from the Figure 2 footnote, under which three most-frequent-use estimates were not adjusted for other drug use.

claims.note: Moore does not say in so many words that the cohorts did not record cannabis type; it follows from the exposure definitions (ever use, past-year use, frequency, dependence; Figures 1-2) and the Discussion's remark that cannabinoid content varies by source and intake practice and self-reported frequency is error-prone. 'Pooled to 2006' is right (search to 5 September 2006, p. 319).

anchors.extracted: Exposures in the seven cohorts were ever use (past-year use in NPMS) and, for the frequency analysis, daily use (CHDS, ECA, EDSP), weekly use (NEMESIS), more than 50 occasions (Swedish conscripts) or dependence (NPMS); no exposure defined by cannabis type, THC or CBD content.

anchors.locator: Discussion, right column, last paragraph (continuing on p. 326)
anchors.extracted: Measuring cannabis use is hard: biologically available cannabinoid concentrations vary widely with the source of cannabis and the way it is taken, and self-reported frequency is error-prone; random misclassification would usually hide an association, differential misclassification could inflate it.

claims.overstatement: Mild: Moore does not make the time-lag point on its own data; it reports what 'other projections' suggest, citing ref. 61 (Hickman et al., 2007, model projections for England and Wales), which is probably the same British modelling study the claim already lists ('too early to see any rise in England and Wales'). 'The 2007 systematic review adds' presents a citation as the review's own contribution and may make one modelling study look like two sources.
claims.note: The same paragraph also reports that projected schizophrenia trends have not paralleled cannabis trends and that this mismatch has been used as an argument against causation (ref. 60, Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003, the Australian modelling study), consistent with the claim's 'studies disagree'. Second-hand throughout, as the claim says.

anchors.locator: Discussion, left column, paragraph beginning 'Projected trends for schizophrenia incidence' (ends at top of right column)
anchors.extracted: Projected schizophrenia incidence has not tracked rising cannabis use, which has been used as an argument against a causal effect (ref. 60); other projections (ref. 61, England and Wales) suggest that time lags and a lack of reliable incidence data may mean changes are not yet visible.

key_findings.note: 10 databases, to 5 Sept 2006, 4804 references, 175 (3.6%) full texts, 143 excluded, 11 psychosis reports from 7 cohorts and 24 affective reports from 15 cohorts, all as printed (pp. 319-320).

All seven cohort ORs, the pooled 1.41 (1.20-1.65), p = 0.28, I2 19.2% and Egger p = 0.48 match Figure 1 (p. 320) and p. 321 on the rendered pages; the editors' count of four intervals excluding 1 and six point estimates above 1 is right (NPMS 0.72 is the exception).
Figure 2 values, pooled 2.09 (1.54-2.84), I2 44.1%, sensitivity 1.92 (1.50-2.47), I2 25.0%, and the footnote on EDSP, NEMESIS and NPMS checked on rendered p. 321.
COMT crude ORs 10.9 (2.2-54.1) and 1.1 (0.21-5.4), only with first use before 18 (p. 321); 'very weak' (p. 325).
Values and the 44.3% mean confirmed (same calculation). See 'missed': the contrast behind each Table 1 percentage is not stated, and the NPMS 80% cannot come from the Figure 1 ever-use estimate.
15 cohorts and Egger p = 0.13 are on p. 322; the rest, Figure 4 values and pooled 1.49 (1.15-1.94), I2 29.6%, on p. 323.
The statement that crude estimates increased in two studies (refs 41, 49) is in the Discussion on p. 325; Table 2 on p. 324 shows the same (ECA 215% increase; Baltimore 40% decrease to 60% increase).
Levin's formula recomputed: 0.4 x 0.41 / 1.164 = 14.1%; with 1.20 and 1.65, 7.4% and 20.6%, as the card says.
Table 3 also lists Macleod et al. (2004), a systematic review without meta-analysis; the finding rightly names only the three syntheses with pooled estimates.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in the blind reading (p. 325 vs Figure 2 footnote, p. 321).
Ref. 10 is Renault et al. (1974), a human laboratory study (p. 327); the suicidality sentence on p. 323 cites it as one of four cohorts.
Recounted: 11 psychosis + 24 affective reports = 35; refs 31 and 32 are in both groups and the NPMS affective data are a personal communication, leaving 32 references, which equals 175 - 143.
Asterisked unadjusted estimates: Figure 3 (NoRMHS, NY schools), Figure 4 (NoRMHS, inside the pooled 1.49), Figure 5 (Chicago), Figure 6 (NoRMHS).
Same recomputation: about 7% to 21% against the printed 7 to 19.
Six and five-plus-one studies on p. 321; seven each on p. 323; refs 35, 41, 42, 44, 45, 51, 52 vs Figure 6 cohorts as described.
Found independently; the authors are THMM, SZ, AL-H, TREB, PBJ, MB and GL.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional): one critical flaw (item 2, no protocol), item 7 not judgeable from the article. The domain judgments match what the article reports; item 11 'yes' is a close call, as the card says, because three of six most-frequent-use estimates lack adjustment for other drugs and the depression pool includes an unadjusted estimate.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible: the summary's 'independently of confounding' covers measured confounders only, and 'similar' understates the disorder estimate (2.58 vs 1.41), but the paper states its uncertainty plainly (pp. 325, 327) and labels the attributable fraction as conditional on causality.

missed.item: Table 1 does not say which exposure contrast each 'crude to adjusted' percentage refers to, and the NPMS value cannot refer to the ever-use estimate pooled in Figure 1: with an adjusted OR of 0.72 the footnote's formula (crude - adjusted)/(crude - 1) gives more than 100% for any crude OR above 1. It fits the dependence estimate in Figure 2 (1.47) with a crude OR of about 3.35. The implied crude ORs for the other six cohorts are plausible with either contrast, so the seven percentages may mix ever-use and most-frequent-use contrasts.
missed.consequence: The 'about 45% (10%-80%)' attenuation is an average over unstated, possibly mixed contrasts; claims may cite it as a description of how much adjustment shrank the cohorts' associations, but should not attach it to the pooled ever-use OR of 1.41 in particular. Suggested as a reporting issue.
